original_value: In recent years, hyperspectral remote sensing (HRS) has become common practice for remote analyses of the physiognomy and composition of forests. Supervised classification is often used for this purpose, but demands intensive sampling and analyses, whereas unsupervised classification often requires information retrieval out of the large HRS datasets, thereby not realizing the full potential of the technology. An improved principal component analysis-based classification (PCABC) scheme is presented and intended to provide accurate and sequential image-based unsupervised classification of Mediterranean forest species. In this study, unsupervised classification and reduction of data size are performed simultaneously by applying binary sequential thresholding to principal components, each time on a spatially reduced subscene that includes the entire spectral range. The methodology was tested on HRS data acquired by the airborne AisaFENIX HRS sensor over a Mediterranean forest in Mount Horshan, Israel. A comprehensive field-validation survey was performed, sampling 257 randomly selected individual plants. The PCABC provided highly improved results compared to the traditional unsupervised classification methodologies, reaching an overall accuracy of 91%. The presented approach may contribute to improved monitoring, management, and conservation of Mediterranean and similar forests.

result.paraphrase: In recent years, hyperspectral remote sensing (HRS) has become a standard tool for remote analysis of forest physiognomy and composition. Although supervised classification is commonly applied, it requires extensive sampling and analysis; unsupervised methods, meanwhile, often rely on information retrieval from large HRS datasets and therefore fail to exploit the technology’s full potential. This work introduces an improved principal component analysis-based classification (PCABC) scheme designed to deliver accurate, sequential, image-based unsupervised classification of Mediterranean forest species. The study performs unsupervised classification and data reduction at the same time by using binary sequential thresholding on principal components, each applied to a spatially reduced subscene covering the full spectral range. The method was evaluated using HRS data collected by the airborne AisaFENIX HRS sensor over a Mediterranean forest in Mount Horshan, Israel. A thorough field-validation survey sampled 257 randomly selected individual plants. Compared with conventional unsupervised classification methods, the PCABC produced markedly better results, achieving 91% overall accuracy. This approach may help improve the monitoring, management, and conservation of Mediterranean and comparable forests.
